Abstract: Effective management of recreational fisheries requires accurate forecasting of future harvests and real-time monitoring of
ongoing harvests. Traditional methods that rely on historical catch data to predict short-term harvests can be unreliable,
particularly if changes in management regulations alter angler behavior. In contrast, statistical modeling approaches can
provide faster, more flexible, and potentially more accurate predictions, enhancing management outcomes. In this study,
we developed and tested models to improve predictions of Gulf of Mexico gag harvests for both pre-season planning and
in-season monitoring. Our best-fitting model outperformed traditional methods (i.e., estimates derived from historical
average harvest) for both cumulative pre-season projections and in-season monitoring. Notably, our modeling framework
appeared to be more accurate in more recent, shorter seasons due to its ability to account for effort compression. A
key advantage of our framework is its ability to explicitly quantify the probability of exceeding harvest quotas for any
given season duration. This feature enables managers to evaluate trade-offs between season duration and conservation
goals. This is especially critical for vulnerable, highly targeted stocks. Our findings also underscore the value of statistical
models to complement and advance traditional fisheries management approaches.
Key words: Gag, Gulf of Mexico, Season projections, Effort compression, Fishing season, In-season monitoring

Abstract
Effective management of recreational fisheries requires accurate forecasting of future harvests and real-time monitoring of
ongoing harvests. Traditional methods that rely on historical catch data to predict short-term harvests can be unreliable,
particularly if changes in management regulations alter angler behavior. In contrast, statistical modeling approaches can
provide faster, more flexible, and potentially more accurate predictions, enhancing management outcomes. In this study,
we developed and tested models to improve predictions of Gulf of Mexico gag harvests for both pre-season planning and
in-season monitoring. Our best-fitting model outperformed traditional methods (i.e., estimates derived from historical
average harvest) for both cumulative pre-season projections and in-season monitoring. Notably, our modeling framework
appeared to be more accurate in more recent, shorter seasons due to its ability to account for effort compression. A
key advantage of our framework is its ability to explicitly quantify the probability of exceeding harvest quotas for any
given season duration. This feature enables managers to evaluate trade-offs between season duration and conservation
goals. This is especially critical for vulnerable, highly targeted stocks. Our findings also underscore the value of statistical
models to complement and advance traditional fisheries management approaches.
Key words: Gag, Gulf of Mexico, Season projections, Effort compression, Fishing season, In-season monitoring
Introduction
One of the primary management strategies in recreational
fisheries is the use of temporal harvest restrictions to reduce
fishing pressure. Annual fishing quotas, determined in large
part by stock assessments,
are used to help establish the
duration of the fishing season [24]. The actual duration of
the recreational fishing season is based on projections of when
the quota will be exceeded. Therefore, the accuracy of these
projections,
along with in-season monitoring as the season
progresses, is crucial to minimizing the risk of overfishing and
ensuring sustainable fisheries.
Both preand in-season harvest projections are typically
estimated
using
historical,
temporally
indexed
harvest
information from previous years [2]. Recreational fishing season
closure dates are often established before the season begins
to provide private anglers and for-hire businesses with a clear
expectation of the total season duration. This approach relies
on projections for when the recreational quota will be met
before any harvest data from the present year are available.
[11, 12]. Additionally, temporally indexed recreational harvest
estimates are seldom available on timelines required for inseason management [3, 27]. Due to the substantial number

harvest is often estimated using sampling data from dockside
interviews and mail surveys of effort,
followed by surveybased extrapolation methods [27, 25]. The time required to
implement this methodology, especially the mail survey, results
in estimate reporting lags of up to several months after
sampling. Consequently, managers are often forced to rely on
limited in-season and past harvest information to formulate and
update harvest forecasts as the season progresses.
Unfortunately,
past harvest data can be an unreliable
predictor of future harvest rates when regulations change [3].
Angler behaviors, including decisions about whether to fish
and which species to target, are heavily influenced by fishing
regulations [12, 19]. Anglers often focus on popular species
that are currently open for harvest, and may concentrate their
efforts on a particular species if its season is shortened [1, 41].
When harvests exceed projections based on past estimates,
managers may need to implement post-hoc accountability
measures,
such as reducing the quota for the subsequent
year [i.e.,
a payback; 24].
Participants in the recreational
fishery may perceive these measures as punitive, despite their
adherence to regulations,

socioeconomic factors, weather conditions, and internet search

The accuracy gap between harvest projections based on
statistical models and those derived from traditional methods
may be most pronounced during stock rebuilding periods
when recreational quotas are low and seasons are significantly
shortened.
Managers typically reduce season durations to
alleviate fishing pressure on vulnerable stocks. However, anglers
may respond by intensifying their effort within the limited
fishing window,
leading to increased harvest rates [1, 12].
This phenomenon, known as “effort compression”, has been
widely documented in the recreational Gulf red snapper fishery
[e.g., 30, 31, 40, 12, 19],
where federal season reductions
from 194 days in 2005 to just nine days in 2014 resulted
in exponentially higher catch rates for both private and forhire sectors [see Fig. 4 in 12]. Effort compression is most
pronounced during the shortest seasons, typically when a stock
is overexploited.
Consequently,

behavior can lead to substantial harvest overages precisely when

statistical modeling approaches

theoretically leading to more accurate forecasts and improved

been applied in management settings [12].

Methods
Data sources
We compiled recreational gag harvest data for the for-hire
sector from the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS)
Marine Recreational Information Program (MRIP) For-Hire
Telephone Survey (FHTS) combined with data from the Angler
Point Access Intercept Survey (APAIS) and private recreational
data from the Florida Fish and Wildlife (FWC) State Reef Fish
Survey (SRFS). This approach aligns with the data sources
currently used for gag management, as both the Council and
NOAA NMFS monitor recreational gag landings using SRFS
and FHTS/APAIS data.
Since 2023, the annual recreational gag quota has been
determined based on the most recent stock assessment [34]
in conjunction with a stock rebuilding framework [14] both
of which fundamentally rely on recreational landings from
the private fleet (represented by SRFS) and the for-hire fleet
(represented by FHTS). Aggregated monthly landings from
these surveys are used to monitor quota attainment.
We
applied similar aggregation methods to construct our predictive
models, with two exceptions. First, although MRIP collects
data from shore-based anglers and includes shore harvest in the
recreational quota, we excluded shore mode from our analysis
due to its historically negligible contribution to gag landings
and the high uncertainty in its estimates [28]. Second, our
analysis focused on the west coast of Florida only (excluding
the Florida Keys) rather than the Gulf as a whole, as more
than 98% of all Gulf gag landings have occurred in Florida
since 2011 [28, 14].

Both SRFS and FHTS use dockside sampling to collect
catch-per-trip data.
In these interviews,
trained samplers
record details from anglers about their completed fishing trips,
including the number and species of fish caught,
the size
of landed fish, and fishing effort (e.g., hours fished). These
catch data are then combined with effort estimates from the
mail or telephone surveys to calculate total harvest. Statistical

and potential reporting biases, ensuring robust estimates for
fisheries management. To standardize harvest rates from SRFS
and FHTS in Florida, we aggregated monthly gag harvest
estimates across months with varying open seasons. We then
divided each monthly estimate by the number of days open to
fishing to calculate daily harvest rates. To avoid division by zero
in months when harvest was closed, we added one additional
day to the denominator.
Predictors considered
We considered multiple regulatory, social, and environmental
predictors to model patterns in recreational gag harvest rates
(Table 1). Fundamentally, we expected gag harvest rates to
be positively related to whether a month was open to gag
harvest, as anglers would presumably target gag when the
season is open [20]. However, gag temporal regulations along
the Gulf Coast of Florida are complex and have historically
differed spatially, requiring careful consideration of how to
translate these regulations into relevant predictors. From 2012
to 2022, a four-county special season for gag in Florida applied
during late winter and early spring. This special season
included gages with a history of high catch and closed the
gag season to private and for-hire anglers during the preceding
months. This system was implemented to allow for increased
catch during the season, but private and for-hire anglers were
not permitted to fish until the season closed. However, during
2023 and 2024, the GMFMC reduced the season duration to
49 days in 2023 and 15 days in 2024, significantly impacting
the timing of CPUE estimates. Additionally, the social
environment, including social media sentiment, was considered
as a potential driver of fishing behavior. We also considered
a range of environmental variables, such as sea surface temperature
(SST), seasonal rainfall, and sea surface
chlorophyll
concentration
[17, 19, 20, 21, 30, 31, 32].
Table 1 lists the variables we used as predictors in our
statistical models. The variables included both time-varying
and time-invariant factors. Time-varying factors were monthly
in origin, while time-invariant factors were region-specific
and constant across the study period. The approach used
was to fit a regression model for each month of the year,
wherein each model included the same set of predictors but
with time-varying covariates lagged appropriately to account
for temporal dependencies. We applied a mixed-effects
model with a year as a random effect to account for year-to-year
variability in the response variable.
Model
validation
We evaluated the models using cross-validation techniques,
splitting the data into training and validation sets to
assess the models' performance in predicting out-of-sample
harvest. The root mean square error (RMSE) and mean
absolute error (MAE) were used as metrics for model
accuracy. Cross-validation was performed using a 10-fold
splitting method, with each fold representing a unique year
of data. The models were trained on 90% of the data, with
10% reserved for validation. We used the validation sets to
tune hyperparameters, such as regularization strength, to
maximize model performance across different folds.
We also assessed the models' ability to predict seasonally
varying harvest rates by comparing predicted values to
actual observed values across the entire dataset. Additionally,
we examined the residuals for autocorrelation and heteroscedasticity
to ensure the assumptions of the regression model were
met.
Results
Pre-season projection
We found that our statistical models outperformed
the traditional method of using historical average harvest
estimates for both cumulative pre-season projections and
in-season monitoring. The models were particularly accurate
in the most recent years and in shorter seasons, where effort
compression was most pronounced.
In the pre-season, the models predicted cumulative
harvest based on monthly estimates, summing these estimates
over the season duration. We compared these predictions to
the actual cumulative harvest for the season, which was
available from the SRFS and FHTS data.
The models achieved
a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.25 pounds per day (ppd)
and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.33 ppd for
pre-season projections, compared to the traditional method's
MAE of 0.35 ppd and RMSE of 0.45 ppd.
In-season monitoring
During the in-season period, the models provided monthly
estimates of harvest rates, which were used to track when
the cumulative harvest reached the quota limit. We compared
the model's predicted monthly CPUE to the actual monthly
CPUE from the data sources. The models' MAE was 0.20 ppd,
and RMSE was 0.28 ppd, compared to the traditional method's
MAE of 0.23 ppd and RMSE of 0.30 ppd.
Discussion
While the traditional method of using historical averages
performed adequately in some cases, the statistical models
developed here demonstrated superior accuracy in both pre-
season projection and in-season monitoring, especially during
shortened seasons with high effort compression. The models
incorporated key variables such as season duration, environmental
conditions, and social media sentiment, which allowed for
more precise quantification of the risk of exceeding harvest
quotas. This enhanced the ability of managers to formulate
and update catch-and-effort limits dynamically, leading to
more sustainable and resilient fishery management practices.
Additionally, the models' ability to account for effort compression
enabled more accurate harvest forecasts, which are critical for
effective management decisions, especially when dealing with
highly variable and overexploited stocks like the Gulf gag.
Conclusion
